title: Why we model returns, not prices
objectives: Compare a price series with its returns and see which one is stable.
Explain why models are fitted to returns and not prices.

screens.title: Which one repeats itself?
screens.prose: A seeded share price, one close a day from 2016 to 2023: 2,000 days. Top: the price. Bottom: its daily return, in %. A model learns from the shaded years, 2016 to 2018.
screens.question: Which panel shows values in 2023 that look like the values the model learnt from?

options.text: The returns
The price
options.why: You read the price's wiggles as familiar. Its 2023 closes run from £218 to £256; the training closes never passed £161.

options.text: Both of them
options.why: The returns look alike, but the price does not. Every 2023 close is above the highest training close, £161.42.

options.text: Neither of them
options.why: Look at the bottom panel again. The 2023 returns sit in the same band around 0 as the 2016 ones.

hints.text: Compare the left end of each panel with its right end.
Look at the training shade on the price, then at 2023.
Training prices stay between £99 and £161. The 2023 prices are all above £218. The returns stay in about ±3% throughout.

feedback.correct: That's it. The returns in 2023 look like the returns in 2016; the prices do not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each panel: would a typical 2016 value look typical in 2023?

byKey.price: You took the price for stable. Every 2023 close is above £161, the training maximum.
byKey.both: You treated both panels alike. Only the bottom one returns to the same band.

explain.text: Training closes lie between £98.82 and £161.42; every 2023 close lies above £217.58. So the price's level in 2016 says nothing about 2023. The daily return's sd was 1.19% in training and 1.29% in 2023.

screens.title: Where does a price go?
screens.prose: The same kind of path, twenty times: each day adds 0.03% plus noise with sd 1.2% to the log price. The dashed lines are two sds either side of the drift. Draw new paths a few times.
screens.question: Where will a path be after 1,000 days?

options.text: Anywhere in a band that keeps widening
Back near where it started
options.why: You expected a pull back to the start. Nothing in the rule pulls a path back: each day adds fresh noise to wherever it is.

options.text: Near the average of its first 250 days
options.why: You used the early days as a centre. Draw new paths: many leave that level and never come back.

options.text: At the same level each time
options.why: Draw new paths again. The end points move a lot from batch to batch.

hints.text: Press New paths three times and watch the right-hand end.
The dashed lines are $\pm 2\sigma\sqrt{t}$ around the drift. Follow the bold path.
At day 1,000 the band is $\pm 2 \times 1.2\sqrt{1000} \approx \pm 76\%$ wide, and still growing.

feedback.correct: Correct. The spread grows like $\sqrt t$, so no level is typical.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Draw new paths and watch where they end.

explain.text: After $t$ days the log price has sd $1.2\sqrt t$ %: 38% after 1,000 days and 54% after 2,000. A path has no level to return to. Its mean over one stretch says nothing about the next (Markov Chains, lesson 12).

screens.title: Stationary
screens.prose: Cut the hook's 2,000 days into four blocks of about 500. The table shows each block's mean and sd. A series whose mean and spread stay put through time is **stationary** (Financial ML, lesson 5).

state.caption: Price blocks climb from £116 to £228. Return blocks barely move.

screens.question: Complete `summary_stats_by_block(x, n_blocks)`: one row per block, in time order, holding the block mean and the sample sd.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_price(seed, n=2000):
    """Seeded daily closes from £100: a random walk in log price,
    drift 0.03% and sd 1.2% a day."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    r = 0.0003 + 0.012 * rng.standard_normal(n - 1)
    return 100 * np.exp(np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(r)]))

Replace the two dots with `b.mean()` and `b.std(ddof=1)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. The price's block means climb by about £110; the return's stay within 0.03 percentage points.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. One row per block: the mean first, then the sd with `ddof=1`.

explain.text: The price's block mean doubles across the sample, while its block sd stays smaller than the gaps between means. The return's means and sds barely move. That is the line between a series history can describe and one it cannot.

screens.title: From prices to returns
screens.prose: The daily **log return** is $r_t = \ln(p_t / p_{t-1}) = \ln p_t - \ln p_{t-1}$. From $n$ prices you get $n - 1$ returns. Day $t$'s return needs day $t - 1$'s close, so the first day has none.
screens.question: Complete `log_returns(prices)` so element $k$ is the return from day $k$ to day $k + 1$.

screens.title: Today against yesterday
screens.prose: To ask how much today's price depends on yesterday's, regress $x_t$ on $x_{t-1}$. First line the data up: each row pairs a close with the close before it.
screens.question: Fill the $x_{t-1}$ column. Then estimate the slope of the best line through the pairs, to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Day 2's $x_{t-1}$ is day 1's close.
Each close is within £3 of the one before.
The lag column reads 100, 102, 99, 97, 96. The pairs hug the line $x_t = x_{t-1}$, so the slope is close to 1: least squares gives 0.99.

feedback.correct: Correct. The lag column is the close column moved down one row, and the slope is 0.99.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each $x_{t-1}$ is the close one row up; the slope is near 1 when each close sits close to the one before.

explain.text: Least squares on the five pairs gives $x_t = -0.33 + 0.9912\,x_{t-1}$. A slope near 1 says today's price is roughly yesterday's: the level carries over, almost unchanged. Lesson 3 calls a slope of exactly 1 a **unit root**.

import numpy as np

def lag_slope(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    prev, today = x[:-1], x[1:]
    return np.polyfit(prev, today, 1)[0]

screens.title: An R² of 0.998
screens.prose: A colleague regresses the hook's price on yesterday's price. The fit is superb: $R^2 = 0.9977$. "Yesterday's price explains 99.8% of today's. We can predict it." Left: today against yesterday. Right: the same for returns.
screens.question: What is wrong with the claim?

options.text: A random walk gives the same $R^2$: it measures how the level carries over, not any edge on the change
Nothing: an $R^2$ of 0.998 means strong prediction
options.why: You read $R^2$ as predictive power. This price is a seeded random walk: its next change is pure noise, and the fit is still 0.998.

options.text: Use log prices instead, and then the claim holds
options.why: You treated the log price as stationary. It is a random walk too: its lag slope is 0.9987 and its $R^2$ is 0.9981.

options.text: The $R^2$ should be computed out of sample
options.why: Out of sample it is still about 0.99, because the walk carries its level over. The problem is what $R^2$ measures here.

hints.text: How was this price made? Could its change be predicted?
Compare the left cloud with the right one.
Predicting today's price with yesterday's is right to within a day's move. Any walk, predictable or not, does that.

feedback.correct: Correct. The $R^2$ comes from the level, which any random walk carries over.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what an unpredictable walk would score on the same regression.

byKey.fine: You read $R^2$ as predictive power. The price's change is pure noise by construction, yet the fit is 0.998.
byKey.logs: You took logs to make the price stationary. A log price is still a random walk, with the same near-perfect fit.

explain.text: Today's price is yesterday's plus a small change, so the cloud hugs the diagonal whatever the change does. The right panel asks the real question, whether yesterday's move predicts today's: $R^2 = 0.0003$. A trader profits from the change, never from the level.

screens.title: Two exceptions
screens.prose: Top: a seeded bond price trading near its par value of £100, pulled back to par every time it strays. Bottom: a seeded daily return series, in %, from a market that turned stormy on day 250.
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: The bond's price level can be modelled directly: it keeps returning to £100
The return series is not stationary: its spread jumps on day 250
Every return series is stationary, so the bottom one is too
options.why: You treated stationary as a property of returns. It is a property of a series: here the sd triples halfway through.

options.text: Every price must be turned into returns before modelling
options.why: You applied the rule to a price with a fixed centre. The bond's level has a mean, £100, that history can estimate.

hints.text: For each panel, ask: do the mean and the spread stay put?
Look at the bottom panel either side of day 250.
The bond has a fixed centre, par. The returns keep a mean near 0, but their spread jumps from about 0.7% to 2.2%.

feedback.correct: Correct. A price can be stationary, and a return series can fail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge each series by its own mean and spread, not by whether it is a price or a return.

byKey.allret: You assumed every return series is stationary. This one's sd triples on day 250.
byKey.allprice: You differenced by reflex. The bond already has a fixed mean, so its level is modellable.

explain.text: A bond near par, or a spread between two related prices, has a level it keeps returning to: that is the subject of the Cointegration course. A return series with a volatility regime has a steady mean but a shifting spread, which the GARCH course models. Stationarity is checked, never assumed.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: The price's block means climbed and its lag slope was about 1. The return's block means and sds stayed put, and its lag slope was about 0. So we model $$r_t = \ln p_t - \ln p_{t-1},$$ whose distribution history can estimate, and rebuild prices from it: $p_t = p_0\, e^{r_1 + \dots + r_t}$.
screens.question: Which can a model safely learn from 2016 to 2018 and use in 2023?

options.text: The sd of daily log returns
The average closing price
options.why: You kept a level. The 2016 to 2018 average price, about £126, is far below every 2023 close.

options.text: The range the price trades in
options.why: You kept a level's range. The 2023 prices lie entirely above the training range.

options.text: The lag slope of the price, for forecasting changes
options.why: You kept the price regression. Its slope of about 1 only says the level carries over; it predicts no change.

feedback.correct: Correct. The return sd was about 1.2% in training and 1.3% in 2023.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the quantity whose value did not drift.

explain.text: A return's mean and spread mean the same thing in every year. So last year's estimate is usable next year. Any summary of the price level is tied to the years it came from.

screens.title: Desk A's forecast
screens.prose: Desk A fits the price on its own lag over the training years: $p_t = 0.563 + 0.9961\,p_{t-1}$. Run forward from the last training day, its forecast (dashed) settles at £144.48. The price itself ends at £248.15.
screens.question: Where does £144.48 come from?

options.text: The long-run mean the training fit implies, $a/(1 - b)$
The last training close
options.why: You took the starting point for the target. The last training close was £153.34; the forecast falls from there.

options.text: The average of all 2,000 closes
options.why: You let the model see the test years. It fitted on training only, and the full-sample average is £174.88.

options.text: A coding error: a lag-1 model cannot flatten out
options.why: It flattens because $b < 1$: each step moves the forecast a fraction $1 - b$ of the way to $a/(1 - b)$.

hints.text: Where would the forecast stop moving, so that $p_t = p_{t-1}$?
Set $p = a + bp$ and solve for $p$.

feedback.correct: Correct. With $b$ just below 1, the fit believes in a mean of £144.48, learnt from 2016 to 2018.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the price at which the model's forecast stops changing.

explain.text: A slope just under 1 tells the model the price reverts, slowly, to $a/(1 - b) = £144.48$. That level is an accident of the training years. The model learnt their level, exactly as a tree on prices does (Trees and Ensembles, lesson 4).

screens.title: The two desks, one day ahead
screens.prose: Desk B fits the log return on its own lag, $r_t = c + d\,r_{t-1}$, and turns it into a price: $\hat p_t = p_{t-1} e^{c + d r_{t-1}}$. Both desks forecast one day ahead on every test day. We score them by mean squared error in £².
screens.question: Complete `level_vs_return_fit(prices, n_train)`: return the test-period MSE of Desk A and of Desk B.

import numpy as np

def level_vs_return_fit(prices, n_train):
    p = np.asarray(prices, dtype=float)
    r = np.log(p[1:] / p[:-1])          # r[k]: day k to day k + 1
    # fit on the first n_train closes only
    b, a = np.polyfit(p[:n_train - 1], p[1:n_train], 1)
    d, c = np.polyfit(r[:n_train - 2], r[1:n_train - 1], 1)
    prev = p[n_train - 1:-1]            # yesterday's close, each test day
    level_fc = ...                      # Desk A: a + b * yesterday's close
    return_fc = ...                     # Desk B: yesterday's close times exp(c + d * yesterday's return)
    actual = p[n_train:]
    mse_level = np.mean((actual - level_fc) ** 2)
    mse_return = np.mean((actual - return_fc) ** 2)
    return round(float(mse_level), 4), round(float(mse_return), 4)
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def level_vs_return_fit(prices, n_train):
    p = np.asarray(prices, dtype=float)
    r = np.log(p[1:] / p[:-1])          # r[k]: day k to day k + 1
    b, a = np.polyfit(p[:n_train - 1], p[1:n_train], 1)
    d, c = np.polyfit(r[:n_train - 2], r[1:n_train - 1], 1)
    prev = p[n_train - 1:-1]            # yesterday's close, each test day
    level_fc = a + b * prev
    return_fc = prev * np.exp(c + d * r[n_train - 2:-1])
    actual = p[n_train:]
    mse_level = np.mean((actual - level_fc) ** 2)
    mse_return = np.mean((actual - return_fc) ** 2)
    return round(float(mse_level), 4), round(float(mse_return), 4)

explain.text: On seed 12 the one-day errors are close, 6.5228 against 6.4738: a day ahead, both desks say roughly yesterday's price. On seed 6 the training years were flat, $b$ came out near 0.98, and Desk A's pull towards its training mean makes its error 71% larger. Desk B never claims a level.

screens.title: In the interview
screens.prose: Every model on a desk, from a factor regression to a GARCH, is fitted to returns. The reason in one sentence: **models are fitted to returns because returns are stationary and prices are not.** An interviewer asks you why.
screens.question: Which answer gives the reason and its evidence?

options.text: Returns keep a fixed mean and spread that history can estimate; a price has no fixed mean
Returns are small numbers, so the regressions are better conditioned
options.why: You gave a numerical reason. Scaling a price would fix conditioning and keep the problem: its mean still drifts.

options.text: Prices are not normally distributed and returns are
options.why: You gave a distributional reason. Returns have fat tails too; what matters is that their distribution stays put.

options.text: We are paid on returns, not on prices
options.why: P&L is why we care about returns, but it is not why the fit works. The statistical reason is that returns are stationary.

hints.text: The interviewer wants the statistical property, then the evidence.
Read the evidence table one last time.
Stationary returns: a fixed mean and spread that history can estimate. Non-stationary prices: a drifting level.

feedback.correct: Correct. Returns are stationary and prices are not, so only a model of returns carries from one period to the next.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give the property that makes history usable, and say why the price lacks it.

explain.text: Lead with the sentence, then the evidence: block means that climb, a lag slope of 1, a level the test years never visited. Add the honest caveat that some levels, such as a spread, are stationary, and that return volatility clusters.

ideas: A price has no fixed mean: its spread grows like $\sqrt t$, so one period's level says nothing about the next.
Regressing a price on its lag gives a slope near 1 and an $R^2$ near 1 even for a pure random walk. On returns the slope is near 0.
Models are fitted to returns because returns are stationary and prices are not. Check it: a mean-reverting spread is a stationary level, and a volatility regime breaks a return series.

formula.name: Log return
formula.tex: r_t = \ln p_t - \ln p_{t-1}, \qquad p_t = p_0\, e^{r_1 + \dots + r_t}
formula.note: $n$ prices give $n - 1$ returns, and the returns add up to $\ln(p_n / p_0)$.

summary.trap: An $R^2$ of 0.99 from a price on its lag is not predictive power: a random walk scores the same. Taking logs does not make a price stationary.

quiz.prose: A share closes at £250 one day and £245 the next.
quiz.question: What is the log return? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the log of today over yesterday.

byKey.simple: You gave the simple return, $245/250 - 1$. The log return is $\ln(245/250)$, slightly further from 0.
byKey.flip: You divided yesterday by today. The return runs from yesterday to today, so today goes on top.

explain.text: $\ln(245/250) = \ln 0.98 = -0.0202$. The simple return is $-0.02$; for small moves the two are close.

quiz.prose: A pure coin-flip random walk of 1,000 steps, far from 0, is regressed on its own lag.
quiz.question: What $R^2$ do you expect?

options.text: Close to 1
Close to 0, because the steps are unpredictable
options.why: You applied the step's unpredictability to the level. Each value is the previous one plus a small step, so the fit is near perfect.

options.text: About 0.5
options.why: There is no half-way here: the level carries over almost entirely from one step to the next.

options.text: Negative
options.why: $R^2$ from least squares with an intercept is never negative.

feedback.correct: Correct. The level carries over, so $R^2$ is near 1 with no predictive power at all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how far each value is from the one before it.

explain.text: $x_t = x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ with a small step, so $x_t$ is almost $x_{t-1}$. The fit is near perfect and says nothing about the next step.

quiz.prose: Four candidate series for a model that will run for five years.
quiz.question: Which one is the most reasonable to model as a level, without differencing?

options.text: The yield gap between two bonds from the same issuer, which keeps returning to about 0.4%
The FTSE 100 index level, which has risen over the decade
options.why: You kept a price level. An index drifts with no fixed centre.

options.text: The log of a share price, which moves less than the price
options.why: You treated a log price as stationary. It is a random walk with drift, as the lag slope showed.

options.text: A fund's cumulative P&L, which has a steady daily mean
options.why: You kept a running total. It adds each day's P&L, so it wanders as a price does.

feedback.correct: Correct. A gap that keeps returning to a level has a fixed mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the series that keeps returning to one value.

explain.text: The yield gap has a centre it returns to, like the bond near par: its level is stationary. The other three are sums of daily changes, so they wander.

quiz.prose: A risk model estimates a fund's daily return sd from 2017, a calm year: 0.6%. In 2020 the sd is 2.1%.
quiz.question: What failed?

options.text: The returns were not stationary: their spread changed
The model should have used prices, not returns
options.why: You went back to the level. Prices drift even more; the fix is a model whose variance can change.

options.text: The mean return changed
options.why: The mean may barely have moved. The sd more than tripled.

options.text: Nothing: 2020 was simply unlucky
options.why: A tripled sd for a whole year is a change in the distribution, not one bad draw.

feedback.correct: Correct. Returns can fail stationarity through their variance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two sds.

explain.text: Returns usually have a steady mean, but their spread moves between calm and stormy regimes. Modelling that changing variance is the job of the GARCH course.
